title: Given M sorted lists of numbers, find the Kth smallest number among all of them. Explain the K-way Merge technique, the heap contents, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Kth Smallest Number in M Sorted Lists (Find the Kth Smallest Across Sorted Lists)
keyPoints: Seed a min-heap with the first element of each sorted list, then pop K times to find the Kth smallest
Each heap entry stores the value, the list index, and the element index so you can push the next element from the same list
The heap holds at most M entries (one per list), not K or N, which bounds space to O(M)
Time complexity is O(K log M) because each of K pops does a log-M heap operation
This is the K-way Merge pattern stopped early at the Kth removal
Guard K against the total element count to avoid over-popping an exhausted set of lists
The same engine fully run produces the merged sorted list of all M lists

s1_definition.oneliner: Pop the global minimum K times from a size-M min-heap; the Kth pop is the answer.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **K-way Merge** – a pattern for merging M sorted sequences using a min-heap of size M that always holds the current smallest unprocessed element from each list.
- **Kth Smallest across M lists** – stop the merge after K pops instead of running it to completion.
- **Heap entry** – stores the value, the list index, and the element index within that list so the next element can be fetched after a pop.
- **Time complexity** – O(K log M) because each of K pops involves a log-M heap operation.
- **Space complexity** – O(M) for the heap, since each list contributes at most one live candidate.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has M branch offices, each with a sorted list of customer fees. Priya wants the Kth cheapest fee across all branches. A clerk keeps one card per branch on a desk, each showing that branch's cheapest unseen fee. The clerk removes the cheapest card, then replaces it with the next fee from the same branch. After K removals, the last card taken is the Kth cheapest fee overall.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Smallest in M Sorted Lists is the K-way Merge pattern stopped early. Because the lists are individually sorted, the Kth smallest value is revealed exactly when you have removed K elements in global sorted order. You seed a min-heap with the first element of every list, each entry remembering which list it came from and its position, then pop K times and after every pop push the successor from the same list.

The reason this is efficient is that you never materialise the full merge. The heap holds at most M candidates, one live element per list, so each pop is O(log M) and K pops cost O(K log M) with O(M) space. The entry must carry the list index and element index so you can fetch the next element cheaply.

At the National Bank of India, the analytics team needed the Kth cheapest fee across dozens of branches, each with pre-sorted fee data. Rather than merging millions of fees, the K-way merge heap advanced only K steps, making the percentile query fast and memory-efficient even at scale.

A senior engineer knows that this is the same engine as Merge K Sorted Lists, simply halted at the Kth removal, and that the heap is bounded by the number of lists rather than by K or N. Explaining this distinction is what shows an interviewer you truly understand the K-way Merge pattern.

Remember one sentence: seed one element per list into a min-heap, pop K times, and the Kth pop is the Kth smallest across all lists.
